{{distinguish|Dini–Lipschitz criterion|Dini's theorem}}
In mathematics, '''Dini's criterion''' is a condition for the [[pointwise convergence]] of [[Fourier series]], introduced by {{harvs|txt|authorlink=Ulisse Dini|last=Dini|first=Ulisse | year=1880}}.

==Statement==
Dini's criterion states that if a [[periodic function]] <math>f</math> has the property that <math>(f(t)+f(-t))/t</math> is [[Locally integrable function|locally integrable]] near <math>0</math>, then the Fourier series of <math>f</math> converges to <math>0</math> at <math>t=0</math>.

Dini's criterion is in some sense as strong as possible: if <math>g(t)</math> is a positive continuous function such that <math>g(t)/t</math> is not locally integrable near <math>0</math>, there is a continuous function <math>f</math> with <math>|f(t)|\leq g(t)</math> whose Fourier series does not converge at <math>0</math>.
